clue.text: "Why, what a hath heaven lent us here!" (King John)

definitions.text: "Why, what a hath heaven lent us here!" (King John)

parts.words: "Why, what a hath heaven lent us here!" (King John)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: in King John the Bastard Faulconbridge greets the Dauphin's defiant envoy with this line, and the missing noun names a wild, reckless fellow

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's King John with one word blanked out, for the solver to restore.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-quotation clue: the gap after 'a' takes a word for an impulsive, hot-headed person, which is how the speaker sizes up the brash young Dauphin's message.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is an old term for a wild, impetuous person, exactly the sort heaven has 'lent' in the speaker's sarcastic exclamation.

clue.text: She could not tell "vat is baiser en Anglish"

definitions.text: She could not tell "vat is baiser en Anglish"

parts.words: She could not tell "vat is baiser en Anglish"
parts.note: points to the wooing scene in Henry V, where Princess Katherine's lady-in-waiting interprets for King Henry and admits she cannot translate the French word for kiss

explanation.surface: A Frenchwoman struggling with English is stumped by the word for a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry V, Act 5, the interpreter for Katherine says 'I cannot tell vat is baiser en Anglish' when Henry asks what the princess means about kissing before marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: The lady-in-waiting who acts as interpreter in Henry V bears this name, and the quoted line is hers.

clue.text: Scene of dramatic homicide

parts.note: refers to T. S. Eliot's verse drama about the killing of Thomas Becket at Canterbury, whose title names the building where the murder happens

explanation.surface: A crime-report phrase for where a theatrical killing took place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dramatic' reads as 'sensational' but means 'in a play': Eliot's Murder in the ___ is set in Canterbury's great church.
explanation.definitionFit: Becket was murdered in Canterbury's great church, the setting named in the title of Eliot's play about him.

clue.text: A bit of a subject for Bulwer-Lytton

definitions.meaning: a type of curb bit for a horse, combining snaffle and curb
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's 1828 novel is titled after its gentleman hero, so he is the novel's subject

explanation.surface: A small portion of something Bulwer-Lytton wrote about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a subject' reads as 'part of a topic', but splits into two senses: a horse's bit, and the hero of Bulwer-Lytton's novel 'Pelham, or the Adventures of a Gentleman'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a kind of horse's curb bit and the title hero of a Bulwer-Lytton novel.

clue.text: Eliot's wife-beater somehow deters MP

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of the following words are put together in some other way, an arrangement signal

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A violent husband in George Eliot puts off a Member of Parliament in some way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges DETERS and MP. In George Eliot's 'Janet's Repentance' (Scenes of Clerical Life) the drunken lawyer Robert Dempster beats his wife Janet.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Dempster is the brutal husband who abuses his wife in George Eliot's story 'Janet's Repentance'.

clue.text: Set piece by Priestley likely to produce a score?

definitions.text: Set piece by Priestley likely to produce a score?

parts.words: Set piece by Priestley likely to produce a score?
parts.note: a play by J. B. Priestley, read as a football set piece from which a goal (a score) may well come

explanation.surface: A theatrical work by Priestley, or a football dead-ball routine that often leads to a goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set piece' means a staged play and, in football, a corner or free kick; 'score' is a goal. Priestley's 1932 play shares its title with a corner kick likely to yield one.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestley's 1932 play has this title, and in football a corner kick that threatens a goal is called this.

clue.text: Margaret Oliphant provided him with a partner

definitions.text: Margaret Oliphant provided him with a partner

parts.words: Margaret Oliphant provided him with a partner
parts.note: alludes to Oliphant's 1869 novel whose title gives a clergyman a spouse, so she literally supplied him with a wife

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist acts as matchmaker for some man.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Oliphant wrote 'The Minister's Wife' (1869): by writing the title she gave the clergyman his partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliphant's novel title pairs a clergyman with his wife, so he is the man she partnered.

clue.text: Spanish circle has short time to discover German violinist ()

parts.note: SP is the standard abbreviation for Spanish
a circle is shaped like the letter O
HR is the abbreviation, a shortened form, of hour

explanation.surface: A Spanish ring needs a brief moment to track down a German fiddler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short time' is the abbreviated hour, HR, not a brief moment. Louis Spohr (1784-1859) was a German violinist and composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Spohr was a celebrated German violin virtuoso and composer of the early Romantic era.

clue.text: Two Syracusans were taken for them, funnily enough

definitions.text: Two Syracusans were taken for them, funnily enough

parts.words: Two Syracusans were taken for them, funnily enough
parts.note: in The Comedy of Errors, Antipholus and Dromio of Syracuse are mistaken for their identical twins, citizens of the town where the comedy is set

explanation.surface: Two visitors from Syracuse were mistaken for locals, comically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funnily enough' points to the play being a comedy: Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors sets the Syracusan twins in Ephesus, where everyone takes them for their local brothers.
explanation.definitionFit: The citizens of Ephesus are the people the visiting Syracusan twins are mistaken for in Shakespeare's comedy.

clue.text: Material for My Beautiful Laundrette supplied by Tom Stoppard?

definitions.text: Material for My Beautiful Laundrette supplied by Tom Stoppard?

parts.words: Material for My Beautiful Laundrette supplied by Tom Stoppard?
parts.note: imagines Stoppard handing over a play title as soiled washing for the laundrette film: his 1976 farce is named after unwashed sheets and private scandal

explanation.surface: Stoppard providing fabric for a famous laundrette film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Material' means fabric to wash, not script material: Stoppard's 1976 farce 'Dirty Linen' is named after the washing a laundrette takes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoppard's farce bears this title, and unwashed sheets and cloths are what a laundrette processes.

clue.text: Strauss baron — very big around church

indicators.note: around says the first piece is placed about the second, enclosing it

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for very big

explanation.surface: A Strauss nobleman is huge round a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very big' is the clothing label for outsize, and 'around' wraps it about the church. Baron Ochs is the boorish cousin in Richard Strauss's opera Der Rosenkavalier.
explanation.definitionFit: Baron Ochs auf Lerchenau is the coarse nobleman in Richard Strauss's opera Der Rosenkavalier.

clue.text: Publicity in serene surroundings for divertimento

indicators.note: in places the publicity piece within the other word

parts.note: the word serene, acting as the surround
an ad is a piece of publicity, an advertisement

explanation.surface: Advertising set amid calm, for a light musical entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' and 'surroundings' together signal the container: 'serene' is the surround and 'Publicity' goes inside. A serenade in Mozart's day was a light suite akin to a divertimento.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are light instrumental suites of several movements, and a serenade in classical usage is a type of divertimento.

clue.text: Poetic accent provided by second part of coiffure

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair, one part of a hairdo

explanation.surface: Verse rhythm found in the back half of a hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second part' looks like 'the latter half', but 'second' is S and 'part of coiffure' is TRESS, a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody the emphasis laid on a syllable is its accent, the beat that metre counts.

clue.text: Spring's encouragement, like fame

definitions.meaning: an incentive that makes one spring into action, as a rider's goad urges a horse forward
Milton's Lycidas says fame is the incentive that 'the clear spirit doth raise'

explanation.surface: Springtime cheer, comparable to renown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' reads as the season but is the verb: what makes a horse spring forward. Milton's Lycidas: 'Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise'.
explanation.definitionFit: An incentive that urges action is this word, and Milton's line names fame as one.

clue.text: Greene's nightingale

parts.note: Robert Greene's 1592 romance 'Lady Fitzwater's Nightingale' takes its heroine's name from the Greek princess turned into that songbird

explanation.surface: A songbird belonging to Greene.
explanation.walkthrough: Greene is the Elizabethan Robert Greene, not Graham: his romance names its virtuous heroine after the princess of Greek myth who became a nightingale.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the ravished princess was turned into a nightingale, and Greene's romance gives her name to his songbird heroine.

clue.text: Some of Arthur Hailey's excess baggage

definitions.text: Some of Arthur Hailey's excess baggage

parts.words: Some of Arthur Hailey's excess baggage
parts.note: one of Hailey's novels (about a power grid strained beyond capacity) is titled with a word for too heavy a burden

explanation.surface: Part of a novelist's surplus luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some of' marks one title among Hailey's many books: his 1979 novel about an electricity crisis has a title meaning an excessive burden.
explanation.definitionFit: Excess baggage is too heavy a burden, and Hailey's 1979 novel takes that word as its title.

clue.text: Part of position taken up by Miss Sobel

definitions.text: Part of position taken up by Miss Sobel

parts.words: Part of position taken up by Miss Sobel
parts.note: Dava Sobel's bestseller is about John Harrison's chronometer and the east-west coordinate of a ship's position at sea

explanation.surface: A woman adopts one element of a stance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'position' reads as a stance or job, but means a location on the globe: Dava Sobel's 1995 book took up the east-west coordinate.
explanation.definitionFit: A position on the globe is given by latitude and its east-west partner, the coordinate Sobel's book is about.

clue.text: Giraudoux's unbalanced dispenser of rough justice in Paris

definitions.text: Giraudoux's unbalanced dispenser of rough justice in Paris

parts.words: Giraudoux's unbalanced dispenser of rough justice in Paris
parts.note: the eccentric Countess Aurelia of Giraudoux's play, who lures greedy financiers into the Paris sewers to their doom

explanation.surface: A deranged Parisian vigilante from a French play.
explanation.walkthrough: Giraudoux's 'The Madwoman of Chaillot' (1945): the crazed Countess Aurelia rids Paris of profiteers by sending them down into the sewers.
explanation.definitionFit: Countess Aurelia, the title heroine of Giraudoux's play, is a crazed woman who takes justice into her own hands.

clue.text: Brendan Behan's hostage

parts.note: in Behan's play The Hostage, the captive is a young British soldier, Leslie, held by the IRA in a Dublin lodging house

explanation.surface: Someone held captive by an Irish playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: In Behan's play 'The Hostage' (1958), the captive is Private Leslie Williams, a British soldier held in a Dublin brothel.
explanation.definitionFit: Leslie Williams is the young English soldier held hostage in Behan's play.

clue.text: New anti-smoking group represents an artist

parts.note: ASH (Action on Smoking and Health) is a British anti-smoking charity

explanation.surface: A fresh campaign against smoking stands for a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: ASH, Action on Smoking and Health, is a British anti-smoking charity. Paul Nash was an English painter, famous for his war landscapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Nash and his brother John were English landscape painters, and John Nash the Regency architect also bears the surname.

clue.text: "Weave the warp, and weave the woof, The winding-sheet of —'s race" (Thomas Gray)

definitions.text: "Weave the warp, and weave the woof, The winding-sheet of —'s race" (Thomas Gray)

parts.words: "Weave the warp, and weave the woof, The winding-sheet of —'s race" (Thomas Gray)
parts.note: a gap in Gray's ode The Bard, where the Welsh bard curses the line of the English king who conquered Wales

explanation.surface: A line from Gray's ode The Bard with a king's name missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'The Bard' the last Welsh bard curses the dynasty of the Plantagenet king who conquered Wales, Edward I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bard curses the descendants of Edward I, the English king who subdued Wales, so his name fills the gap.

clue.text: Appropriate gypsy word-master

definitions.meaning: to take and use as one's own, a verb
George ..., the Victorian writer who studied the Romany language and compiled a Romany word-book

explanation.surface: A fitting master of Romany vocabulary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like the adjective 'fitting' but is the verb 'take'. George Borrow wrote 'Lavengro' and 'Romano Lavo-Lil', a Romany word-book.
explanation.definitionFit: To take something for one's own use is to appropriate it, and George Borrow was the Victorian scholar of the Romany tongue.

clue.text: Gay sports ()

parts.note: John Gay's 1713 georgic poem is titled after the pastimes of the countryside

explanation.surface: Light-hearted games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gay' is the poet John Gay, author of 'Rural Sports' (1713), a georgic dedicated to Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gay's poem 'Rural Sports' describes country pastimes, and the missing word is its adjective for the countryside.

clue.text: Newspaper back number dramatized by Pinter?

definitions.text: Newspaper back number dramatized by Pinter?

parts.words: Newspaper back number dramatized by Pinter?
parts.note: a past issue of The Times, a British daily, is read as the title of a 1971 Pinter play

explanation.surface: An old edition of a paper staged by Pinter.
explanation.walkthrough: A back number is a past issue; of the London newspaper The Times it would be an aged copy, which is the title of Pinter's 1971 play.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinter's 1971 play has this title, which also describes a past issue of The Times newspaper.

clue.text: Occurrence with book supporting first lady ()

indicators.note: in a down entry, the supporting piece sits below the other one, so it comes second

parts.note: Eve was the first woman in Genesis
NT is the New Testament, a book of scripture

explanation.surface: Something happens while a volume props up a president's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first lady' is Eve, not a president's wife; in a down entry 'supporting' places NT below EVE.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is a happening, something that takes place.

clue.text: The one in Defoe's journal was pestilential

definitions.text: The one in Defoe's journal was pestilential

parts.words: The one in Defoe's journal was pestilential
parts.note: Defoe's 'A Journal of the Plague ___' (1722) chronicles London's 1665 outbreak, so the period it covers was plague-ridden

explanation.surface: A period described in Defoe's diary was disease-ridden.
explanation.walkthrough: Defoe's 1722 book 'A Journal of the Plague Year' covers 1665, the twelve months of the Great Plague of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's journal covers twelve months of plague, the period named in its title.

clue.text: Illustrations for an edition of Little Women?

definitions.text: Illustrations for an edition of Little Women?

parts.words: Illustrations for an edition of Little Women?
parts.note: small painted pictures, read as tiny pictures fit for a book whose title is about small females

explanation.surface: Pictures in a printing of Louisa May Alcott's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Women' reads as Alcott's novel but also as a description: tiny portraits of women, painted small, are fitting illustrations.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny detailed paintings, often portraits or manuscript illuminations, are called this, and 'little women' would be just such small pictures.

clue.text: A fable writer

parts.note: read as the author of the 1954 Pulitzer-winning novel 'A Fable', set in the trenches of the First World War

explanation.surface: Someone who writes moral tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A fable writer' reads as an Aesop type, but 'A Fable' is William Faulkner's 1954 novel, which won a Pulitzer Prize.
explanation.definitionFit: William Faulkner wrote 'A Fable' (1954), so he is that book's author.

clue.text: Song from Two Gentlemen of Verona, perhaps

definitions.text: Song from Two Gentlemen of Verona, perhaps

parts.words: Song from Two Gentlemen of Verona, perhaps
parts.note: read not as Shakespeare's play but as two men from an Italian city singing together, which in Italian is a piece for two voices

explanation.surface: A number from Shakespeare's Veronese comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two Gentlemen of Verona' looks like Shakespeare's play, but means two Italian men singing together: an Italian two-voice song.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian word for a piece for two singers, which two Veronese gentlemen would naturally sing.
